title: Is it still good?
keywords: when in doubt throw it out
how long can food sit out
summary: Never taste food to test it, and when in doubt, throw it out. After 4 hours without power or a cold source like ice, throw out the fridge’s perishable food. Refreeze or cook only freezer food that still has ice crystals or is at 40°F (4°C) or below; once the freezer is above 40°F, throw out thawed food. Perishable food left out more than 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F (32°C)) goes. Throw out leaking, bulging or damaged cans and jars, home-canned food you can’t vouch for, and food that touched flood water. A bad smell, color or texture means throw it out; a normal one proves nothing.
doFirst: Never taste food to find out if it is safe (CDC). Throw out any food with an unusual smell, color or texture; a normal one proves nothing: food that looks and smells normal can still make you sick (CDC). When in doubt, throw it out (CDC).

Fridge without power for more than 4 hours, and no cold source like ice? Throw out its perishable food: meat, fish, cut fruits and vegetables, eggs, milk and leftovers (CDC). The chart below goes food by food.

Freezer: refreeze or cook only food that still has ice crystals or is at 40°F (4°C) or below (CDC, FoodSafety.gov). Once the freezer is above 40°F (4°C), throw out thawed food (New York State Department of Health, CDC).

Cans and jars that leak, bulge, are swollen, damaged or cracked, spurt liquid or foam when opened, or hold discolored, moldy or bad-smelling food: throw them out. Don’t eat home-canned food if you don’t know whether safe canning guidelines were followed (CDC).
Throw out food that may have touched flood water or storm water (CDC).

list: Fridge: throw out perishable food (meat, fish, cut fruits and vegetables, eggs, milk and leftovers) after 4 hours without power or without a cold source like ice (CDC). With an appliance thermometer, check that the fridge is still at 40°F (4°C) or below, and check the temperature of food kept in coolers or in a fridge with ice added (CDC).
Food left out: never leave perishable food out for more than 2 hours, or 1 hour if it is above 90°F (32°C) (CDC). Germs multiply fastest between 40°F (4°C) and 140°F (60°C) (FoodSafety.gov).

Freezer: once the freezer is above 40°F (4°C), throw out thawed food (New York State Department of Health, CDC). Food that still has ice crystals or is at 40°F (4°C) or below can be refrozen or cooked (CDC, FoodSafety.gov).
Check each food separately (FoodSafety.gov). How long the fridge and freezer stay cold is in Food when the power goes out.

blocks.label: Food when the power goes out

blocks.p: FoodSafety.gov’s chart for food in the fridge that was at 40°F (4°C) or above for more than 2 hours. Use it as a general guide (FoodSafety.gov). Anything with an unusual smell, color or texture goes, whatever the chart says (CDC).

head: Food in the fridge
At 40°F (4°C) or above for more than 2 hours
rows: Raw or leftover cooked meat, poultry, fish or seafood; soy meat substitutes
Meat, tuna, shrimp, chicken or egg salad
Lunchmeats, hot dogs, bacon, sausage, dried beef
Soft cheeses: blue, Roquefort, Brie, Camembert, cottage, cream, Edam, Monterey Jack, ricotta, mozzarella, Muenster, Neufchatel, queso blanco, queso fresco
Hard cheeses: Cheddar, Colby, Swiss, Parmesan, provolone, Romano
Grated Parmesan, Romano or a mix, in a can or jar
Milk, cream, sour cream, buttermilk, evaporated milk, yogurt, eggnog, soy milk
Fresh shell eggs, eggs hard-cooked in shell, egg dishes, egg products
Dried fruits, raisins, candied fruits, dates
Throw out if above 50°F (10°C) for more than 8 hours
Jelly, relish, taco sauce, mustard, ketchup, olives, pickles
Bread, rolls, cakes, muffins, quick breads, tortillas
Pasta salads with mayonnaise or vinaigrette
Pies with a filling containing eggs or milk (custard, cheese-filled, chiffon); quiche

list: If an appliance thermometer was kept in the freezer, read it when the power comes back on. At 40°F (4°C) or below, the food can be refrozen (USDA).

No thermometer in the freezer? Check each package. Only food that still has ice crystals or is at 40°F (4°C) or below can be refrozen (USDA, FoodSafety.gov) or cooked (CDC). Thawed food in a freezer above 40°F (4°C) goes (New York State Department of Health, CDC).
Refrozen food may lose some quality, but it can still be eaten (USDA, FoodSafety.gov).

blocks.p: FoodSafety.gov’s freezer chart, for food that still has ice crystals and feels as cold as if it were in the fridge. Some of it still goes. Use it as a general guide (FoodSafety.gov). Thawed food is thrown out, as above, even where FoodSafety.gov’s chart would let you refreeze it: New York State Department of Health and CDC say to throw it out, and this app follows the more cautious rule.

head: Food in the freezer
Still has ice crystals and feels as cold as if in the fridge
rows: Eggs (out of shell) and egg products
Vegetables, home or commercially packaged or blanched
Breads, rolls, muffins, cakes without custard filling
Cakes, pies, pastries with custard or cheese filling
Pie crusts, bought or homemade bread dough
Frozen meals, entrees, pizza, sausage and biscuit, meat pie, convenience foods

blocks.warn: Don’t sniff moldy food: it can cause breathing trouble. If food is covered with mold, throw it out (USDA).

blocks.p: USDA’s guide for a spot of mold.

head: Food with mold on it
What to do
rows: Hard salami and dry-cured country hams
Use. Scrub the mold off the surface
Hard cheese (not one where mold is part of how it is made)
Use. Cut off at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) around and below the mold spot, keeping the knife out of the mold. Re-cover the cheese in fresh wrap
Soft cheeses made with mold, such as Brie and Camembert
Throw out if they have mold that is not part of how they are made
Hard cheeses made with mold, such as Gorgonzola and Stilton, with mold on the surface
Cut off at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) around and below the mold spot and handle like hard cheese
Soft cheese (cottage, cream cheese, Neufchatel, chevre and others); crumbled, shredded or sliced cheese of any kind
Firm fruits and vegetables (cabbage, bell peppers, carrots and others)
Use. Cut off at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) around and below the mold spot, keeping the knife out of the mold
Soft fruits and vegetables (cucumbers, peaches, tomatoes and others)
Peanut butter, beans and other legumes, nuts

blocks.p: Any of these signs means home-canned or store-bought food might be contaminated with toxins or harmful germs. Throw it out (CDC):

list: The container is leaking, bulging or swollen.
The container looks damaged, cracked or abnormal.
The container spurts liquid or foam when opened.
The food is discolored, moldy or smells bad.

blocks.p: USDA counts a can as damaged if it is swollen, leaking, punctured, holed, fractured, deeply rusted, or crushed or dented badly enough that it won’t stack or won’t open with a hand-crank opener. Throw out food in damaged cans (USDA).

blocks.warn: You cannot see, smell or taste the toxin that causes botulism, and even a small taste of food that has it can be deadly (CDC). It can be in cans that look normal and in food that smells and tastes normal (New York State Department of Health).

blocks.p: How to get rid of a suspect can or jar without touching what is inside, and the signs of botulism, are in Food poisoning and botulism.

blocks.warn: Don’t eat home-canned food if you don’t know whether safe canning guidelines were followed (CDC).

blocks.p: Home-canned food you know was canned by safe guidelines: CDC says to boil these in a saucepan before eating them, because high temperatures can destroy the toxin that causes botulism:

list: Home-canned tomatoes, and foods that contain them.
All low-acid home-canned foods: all fresh vegetables, figs, meats, poultry, fish, seafood and some tomatoes (CDC).

blocks.p: Below 1,000 feet (300 m), boil them for 10 minutes. Add 1 minute for each 1,000 feet (300 m) higher up (CDC).
Any of the signs under Cans and jars means throw it out, boiled or not (CDC). Refrigerate any canned or pickled food after you open it (CDC).

list: Perishable food that was not kept cold enough because of a power outage.
Food that may have touched flood water or storm water.
Food with an unusual smell, color or texture.
Food in packages that are not waterproof.
Food in cardboard containers, including juice, milk and baby formula boxes.
Food containers with screw caps, snap lids, pull tops, crimped caps, twist caps, flip tops and snap tops (CDC, USDA).
Home-canned food, and cans or food containers that are bulging, open or damaged.
Cans or food containers that spurt liquid or foam when you open them, or hold food that is discolored, moldy or smells bad.
Wooden cutting boards, baby bottle nipples and pacifiers that touched flood water: they can’t be made clean (CDC).

blocks.p: Undamaged, store-bought food in all-metal cans without pull tops, or in retort pouches (flexible, shelf-stable pouches), can be saved (CDC, USDA). Pull-top cans are not waterproof: throw them out (USDA).

steps: Take the labels off if you can, and note the expiration date (CDC, USDA).
Brush or wipe away dirt or silt (CDC, USDA).
Wash the cans and pouches in soapy water, hot if you have it, and rinse them in water that is safe to drink (CDC, USDA).
Put them in a pot of water, bring it to a boil, and keep it boiling for 2 minutes (CDC, USDA).
Let them air-dry for at least 1 hour before you open or store them (USDA).
Re-label each can or pouch with a marker, including the expiration date (CDC, USDA).
Use them as soon as you can (CDC, USDA).

blocks.p: Pans, dishes, utensils and counters that flood water touched (USDA):

steps: Wash metal pans, ceramic dishes and utensils, can openers included, with soap and water, hot if you have it (USDA).
Rinse them, then sanitize them: boil them in clean water, or soak them for 15 minutes in the food mix from Clean and disinfect, which is the strength USDA gives (USDA).
Countertops: wash them with soap and water, hot if you have it, rinse, put the food mix on them, and let them air-dry (USDA).

list: Throw out food that has been near a fire. Heat, smoke fumes and the chemicals used to fight a fire can all damage it (USDA).
Cans and jars may look fine, but the heat of a fire can set off the germs that spoil food. Great heat can split or burst the can or jar (USDA).
Throw out raw food, and food in packaging that lets air through, such as cardboard, plastic wrap, screw-topped jars and bottles (USDA).
Fumes can get into the fridge and freezer too: their seals are not airtight (USDA).
Food that fire-fighting chemicals touched goes in the trash: the chemicals can’t be washed off food (USDA).
Pots and pans that fire-fighting chemicals touched: wash them in soap and hot water, then soak them for 15 minutes in the food mix from Clean and disinfect, which is the strength USDA gives (USDA).

blocks.p: Food that was outdoors during fallout has its own rules: see Water and food after fallout.
